Heat has to leave through the edge, so sustained erasing in an L×L×L grid is capped at about L² nodes per clock.
The two-way binary adder is a ripple: radd takes 2,797 rounds at 4 bits and 5,384 at 8, against relay's 556 and 1,024. A two-way lookahead adder needs extra bits per column.

name: Footprint nets: every rewrite leaves a footprint wired to what it made
angle: Concurrency first. This is an interaction net that can run backward step by step in any order that respects cause and effect. Each agent's only memory is one wire from its back port to the footprint of the rewrite that made it. That wire plays the role of CCSK's shared key and RCCS's per-thread memory, but it is a wire, not a name. Every ready meeting fires at once, forward or backward, and there is no record table. The one lossy step is committing a footprint, which means erasing it.
summary:
It is the current tree-calculus net with one change in meaning. A rewrite does not destroy its two agents. It fuses them into one footprint agent. The footprint keeps the two agents' back wires and is wired to the back port of every agent the rule makes.

That wiring is the run's whole causal history, kept as matter: no table, no ids, no positions read from afar.

- **Going back.** A footprint takes back one product that nothing has used yet, over that product's back wire. This is a two-agent meeting, the same physics as a forward meeting. When every product is back, the footprint splits into its two agents again. So undoing is as local and as parallel as running.
- **Code that should leave no history.** It uses a special case with no footprint, the exchange: a walker and its neighbour change kind in place, and the walker's trail wire is the record.
- **Heat.** Committing a footprint is the one irreversible step and the only heat.

**Prototype** (/tmp/fpnet, scratch Python, no repo files touched):
- It runs all 21 compiled disp calls in research/linear-nets/calls.txt to the eager evaluator's answers, and back to the loaded net agent for agent.
- It also passes 8,000 random terms with random changes of direction.
- Under one scheduler for both tables, going forward takes 0.94–1.08× the current table's rounds. Going back takes 0.55–1.09× the forward rounds.

**Cost.** The history is one footprint per rewrite: 8.7–37× the loaded program.
- Running back every branch that did not reach the answer returns every erased copy as fuel, with no heat.
- What is left beside the answer is only the loaded originals that were dropped without being copied: 24 agents for add 2 3, 83 for fib 3. That is the run's real loss.
- A binary add written as exchanges leaves nothing at all.

**What the angle comes down to.** One idea: the used-up pair is the receipt. And one trade: running many things at once creates history, and history-free code means a single walker, which runs one step at a time.
primitives:
Every agent has three kinds of port:
- a front port p (the principal port), which faces whatever will consume it;
- its other ports;
- a back port b, wired to the footprint that made it. Loaded agents have a capped back port: they have no past.

**Matter (values):**
- L(p): leaf
- S(p, c): stem
- F(p, l, r): fork

**Carriers.** Each one faces what it consumes with its front port.
- A(p = function; z argument, r result): apply.
- T(p = the applied fork's left child x; y = its right child, z, r): first look.
- Q(p = the argument z; arms w, x, y; r): second look, the triage dispatch.
- D(p; o1, o2): copy one layer.
- R(p; o): pass a value on whole.
- N(p; o): read the answer out; this is the root's reader.
- E(p): the collector. It takes a dropped value apart, and every step it takes is recorded.

**Footprint φ(rule, which products are out).** There is one per rewrite. Its ports are:
- the two consumed agents' back wires (its past);
- one child port per product that is out, wired to that product's back port;
- for each product still inside, that product's wires, held as if the product were there.

A footprint has at most 6 wire ends when everything is out, and up to 10 while it is partly taken back (T·S and D·F).

**Other agents:**
- Out(in): the root sink. It has no back port.
- Walkers for two-way code: W(p, t), with a trail port t. Example: the binary adder's carry walker, whose kinds are {down, up} × carry.

**Resources:**
- Fuel is free agent slots and free strands (vacuum).
- Heat is one particle per committed footprint.

**Removed from today's table:** Pair and Unp (T and Q hold their arms directly), P (suspensions; the loader builds A agents), and Seam. Today's eraser Eps becomes the recording collector E.
rules:
**Notation.**
- Every agent also has a back port, which is not written.
- In rules 1–21 the left pair meets front to front. In rules 22–26, E's front port sits on an output port.
- `X(port = wire)` says which of the pair's outside wires a new port takes. ':' separates new agents. a, b, c, d, m, n are new wires between the new agents.

**Carriers meeting matter (18 rules):**
1. A(f,z,r)·L → S(p=r, c=z) [△ z = △z]
2. A·S(x) → F(p=r, l=x, r=z) [△x z = △xz]
3. A·F(x,y) → T(p=x, y, z, r)
4. T(x,y,z,r)·L → R(p=y, o=r) : E(p=z) [K]
5. T·S(s) → D(p=z, o1=a, o2=b) : A(p=s, z=a, r=m) : A(p=y, z=b, r=n) : A(p=m, z=n, r) [S]
6. T·F(w,x) → Q(p=z, w, x, y, r)
7. Q(z,w,x,y,r)·L → R(p=w, o=r) : E(p=x) : E(p=y) [triage, leaf]
8. Q·S(u) → A(p=x, z=u, r) : E(p=w) : E(p=y) [triage, stem]
9. Q·F(u,v) → A(p=y, z=u, r=m) : A(p=m, z=v, r) : E(p=w) : E(p=x) [triage, fork]
10. D(o1,o2)·L → L(p=o1) : L(p=o2)
11. D·S(c) → S(p=o1, c=a) : S(p=o2, c=b) : D(p=c, o1=a, o2=b)
12. D·F(l,r) → F(p=o1, l=a, r=c) : F(p=o2, l=b, r=d) : D(p=l, o1=a, o2=b) : D(p=r, o1=c, o2=d)
13–15. R(o)·L → L(p=o); R·S(c) → S(p=o, c); R·F(l,r) → F(p=o, l, r)
16–18. N(o)·L → L(p=o); N·S(c) → S(p=o, c=a) : N(p=c, o=a); N·F(l,r) → F(p=o, l=a, r=b) : N(p=l, o=a) : N(p=r, o=b)

**The collector (8 rules):**
- 19–21. E·L → nothing; E·S(c) → E(p=c); E·F(l,r) → E(p=l) : E(p=r)
- 22. E on D's o1 → R(p = D's input, o = D's o2), and the mirror image on o2. This un-copies before any copy is made.
- 23. E on A's r → E(p=f) : E(p=z)
- 24. E on T's r → E(p=x) : E(p=y) : E(p=z)
- 25. E on Q's r → E(p=z) : E(p=w) : E(p=x) : E(p=y)
- 26. E on R's o → E(p = R's input)

All 26 were checked in the prototype. The perfect-matching check runs on load. A collector meeting N's output, or two collectors meeting, never happened in 21 programs, so there are no rules for them.

**Laws.** A rule by itself is not a bijection; these laws make it one.
- **meet ↔ part.** Meet: the rule's two agents become one footprint φ(rule, nothing out), holding their outside wires and their two back wires. Part, its inverse: a φ with nothing out becomes the two agents again.
- **emit k ↔ absorb k.** Emit k: φ puts product k into a free slot, wired as the rule says, and the product's back port is wired to φ's child port k. "As the rule says" means: to an outside wire φ holds, to a product that is already out, or back into φ for a product still inside. Absorb k, its inverse: allowed while product k's back port is still wired to φ, that is, while nothing has used it.
- **Why these are bijections.** φ's kind names the rule and which products are out, and nothing else makes it. Forward is meet plus emit each, one block move when there is room. Backward is absorb each, then part. Absorbing is binary: one footprint and one product, over one wire.
- **exchange ↔ itself on the trail.** This is the case with no footprint, for rules whose products already name the pair they came from. A walker W(p, t) and the agent X it faces front to front change kind by a fixed bijection, and each keeps its own back port. W's front moves to X's next agent, and W's trail port t takes X (pointer reversal). The inverse is the same meeting on W's trail wire.
- **commit: the one irreversible, priced law.** A φ with every product out is erased. Its products' back ports are capped (they have no past). The older footprints' child ports that held its two back wires are capped too: those footprints can never split back into their pair, so they may be committed next. Heat is 1 unit, carried off as a particle.
- **Drive.** A meet releases ε and a part takes it back. Nothing else is biased.
resources:
**Copying draws fuel.** A duplicator meeting matter makes the copies in free slots, one layer per meeting, as now. The copy's footprint keeps the two copies linked. So a copy nobody ends up using is taken back by that footprint over its back wire: no comparison, no heat, and the slot comes back. This is Bennett's erasure of one of two copies known to be identical, and Jaynes's mixing of identical gases.
- **Un-copy before copying.** A copy that has not been made yet is never made. A collector that reaches a duplicator's unused output turns the duplicator into a relay. This happened 26,366 times over the 21 calls.
- **Knowing is the footprint.** "What the system knows" is exactly the footprints. While a copy's footprint exists, un-copying is free. After the footprint is committed the twins can no longer be matched, and erasing one costs its information.

**Deleting.** Dropped values are not destroyed: collectors take them apart as recorded meetings. The only real deletion is commit. Erasing a footprint blindly costs 1 unit of heat.
- **The floor.** The minimum is what the footprint knew that the remaining matter does not determine. For a run whose input is still held, that is about 0, because the history is redundant with the input and the machine (Bennett 1973).
- **The gap.** The difference is the price of erasing locally: local control dissipates in proportion to the mutual information it destroys (Boyd, Mandal and Crutchfield). To pay only the floor, run back instead of erasing.
- **Heat as matter.** A committed footprint leaves as a heat particle that diffuses to the edge. So erasing warms its neighbourhood, and erasure throughput is limited by the lattice's surface.

**Drive.** Each meet releases ε and each part takes it back, as in Bennett's Brownian computer. Nothing else is biased. Nothing but commit merges two states into one, so a small ε is enough. Speed costs drive; forgetting costs commit. The two costs are separate.

**Reuse instead of copying:**
- **Matter is reused:** refunds; uncomputed branches return their slots. Running back the branches that missed the answer is garbage collection by a reversed subcomputation (Baker).
- **Work is reused:** speculative work is undone rather than erased.
- **Code is not:** it is still copied layer by layer by the S rule's duplicator. Copying is 28–34% of footprints in most programs (4% in the unrolled relay).
- **An exchange walker is a reused circuit:** the circuit is run along the data, instead of one adder circuit per column.
history_as_resource:
The footprints are the run's history: its occurrence net, held as matter. Programs use it in six ways.

**1. Go back anywhere, in parallel.** Any product nothing has used can be taken back, so any finished part of the run can be undone locally. Measured: going back takes 0.55–1.09× the forward rounds, and the widest backward round holds 171–3,058 steps.

**2. Garbage collection by running back, with no heat.** Run back every branch that did not reach the answer, and keep the answer.
- This removes 20–31% of the footprints.
- It turns every collected copy back into a refund.
- What is left beside the answer is only loaded originals that were dropped without being copied: 24 agents (add 2 3), 65 (rev [1, 2]), 70 (relay_add 255+1), 83 (fib 3), and nothing made by the run. That is the scouts' "real loss" (25 to 112 agents per run), now separated out exactly.
- The other 69–80% of footprints are the answer's own causal past.

**3. Un-copy is free.** A copy's footprint takes back a copy nobody used. A collector that reaches an unmade copy turns the duplicator into a relay, so the copy is never made.

**4. The inverse, prepaid.** A two-way operation that grows the data leaves footprints that are its inverse. Unary add leaves 2|a|+2 footprints, and they are subtraction: drive backward and (a, b) returns with every slot refunded.

**5. History used up by its own program.** Exchange code parks its intermediate state in the data and uses it up on the way back. The binary adder's down sweep leaves each column's carry in that column; the up sweep consumes it while writing the sum. Nothing is left over.

**6. Brownian back-off is free.** Fluctuations can undo recent steps to escape deadlocks, with no record table and no heat.

**When there is none:**
- Loaded agents have no past.
- Committed footprints are gone.
- Exchange code keeps none.

**Honest limit.** Bennett's clean-up (copy the answer, run back) does not work inside the net. Reading uses an agent up, so the answer cannot be kept while its making is undone.
reversible_add:
## Unary

A number n is n forks over a leaf: F(L, F(L, …L)).

**1. disp's compiled `add` on the core** (prototype, measured):
- add 2 3: 2,653 meetings in 896 rounds, answer 5.
- Back to the loaded net agent for agent in 844 rounds, with one product taken back per footprint per round.
- Left: 2,653 footprints, 8.7× the 306 loaded agents.
- Running back the branches that missed the answer removes 518 of them and leaves 24 dropped original agents.

**2. Native: one library carrier G(p = a; o1, o2, t = b).** G copies a, and puts b where the copy's last leaf would be.
- G·F(l,r) → F(p=o1, l=a1, r=c1) : F(p=o2, l=a2, r=c2) : D(p=l, o1=a1, o2=a2) : G(p=r, o1=c1, o2=c2, t)
- G·S(c) → S(p=o1, c=a1) : S(p=o2, c=a2) : G(p=c, o1=a1, o2=a2, t)
- G·L → L(p=o1) : R(p=t, o=o2)

Step by step for a = 2, b = 3:
1. G meets a's top fork. Footprint 1: two forks out, a D on the left leaf, a G on the rest.
2. D meets the leaf. Footprint 2: two leaves.
3. G meets the second fork (footprint 3); D meets its leaf (footprint 4).
4. G meets the last leaf. a keeps that leaf, and an R starts passing b (footprint 5).
5. R meets b's top fork and hands it to a+b (footprint 6).

Result: (a, a+b).
- Fuel drawn: 2|a| new agents, the new spine and its leaves.
- Left over: 2|a|+2 footprints = 6.
- Those footprints only say "these two layers are twins", which (a, a+b) already says. So they are subtraction prepaid.
- Erasing them blindly costs 6 units of heat. It is free in principle for an eraser that checks a against a+b side by side, but that eraser is sequential.
- Checked for a ≤ 10, b ≤ 4: correct, with an exact way back. Depth is about |a|: one walker goes down the spine.
- A version with no footprints would need the twin link itself to be the record. Untested.

## Binary

**3. Compiled relay_add on the core** (measured). Each way back is exact, and each run leaves one footprint per meeting.

| input | meetings | forward rounds | backward rounds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 255+1 (8 bits) | 6,947 | 814 | 531 |
| 65535+1 | 14,429 | 1,105 | 668 |
| 51566+22995 | 14,487 | 1,195 | 660 |

**4. Native, as exchanges, leaving nothing.**

Setup:
- The columns X_ab (one bit of a, one of b; the bits are agent kinds) form a list, least significant first, ending in End.
- A carry walker W starts at the top in the "down" state with carry 0.

The sweeps:
- **Down sweep, at each column:** (c, a, b) → (maj(a,b,c), a⊕c, b⊕c). The walker carries the carry out; the column keeps its carry-in folded into both bits.
- **At End:** W turns from down to up.
- **Up sweep, at each column (a′, b′):** c_i = c ⊕ (a′∧b′), and the column becomes (a′⊕c_i, a′⊕b′⊕c_i) = (a, s).

Both column maps are bijections on 3 bits, so each step is reversible. The trip is 2n+1 exchanges, and the up sweep uses up exactly what the down sweep left (Cuccaro's MAJ down, UMA up).

Left over: nothing. No footprint, no extra agent, the carry is back to 0, and the walker sits at the top marked "done". Even the overflow is absorbed, since (a, a+b mod 2^n) determines it.

Checked: 3,000 random adds up to 12 bits. Every sum is right, the way back is exact, and random back-and-forth followed by going on to the end gives the same sums. It is sequential, with one walker: leaving no history costs parallelism.
tree_calculus:
**Loading.** disp's compiled trees load as matter (L, S, F), with one A per application and N at the root. Loaded agents have no past.

**The rules:**
- **△ z** — A·L builds S.
- **△x z** — A·S builds F.
- **△xy z** — A·F hands x to T, which keeps y and z.
- **K (x = △)** — T·L makes R, which delivers y to the result, and an E on z.
- **S (x = △s)** — T·S makes D on z, A(s z₁), A(y z₂), and A(…, …) joining them. z is copied one layer at a time as it is read, as now. Both halves are wanted, as with today's fork.
- **Triage (x = △w x′)** — T·F makes Q facing the argument. Q·L relays w; Q·S applies x′ to u; Q·F applies y to u and then to v. The two arms not taken each get an E.

**What they leave.** One footprint per meeting, holding the two back wires.
- The footprints of K and triage are also the makers of the E's that take the dropped parts apart, and those E's leave footprints too.
- An E that reaches a duplicator's unused output turns it into a relay before any copy is made: 26,366 times over the 21 calls.
- Measured mix of footprints at the answer: copying 28–34% (4% in the unrolled relay), taking apart 28–39%, apply 15–23%, choosing 11–18%, relaying 10–15%. This matches the scouts' copy, erase and dispatch split.

**What happens to it.** The history can be:
- **kept:** any unused product can be taken back, so any part of the run can go back;
- **uncomputed:** the branches that did not reach the answer run back with no heat, leaving only the dropped loaded originals;
- **committed:** heat.

**Checked:**
- All 21 compiled calls in research/linear-nets/calls.txt give the eager evaluator's answers: fib 3–5, add, mul, is_even, sum, rev, doubled, isort, size, greet, and the ripple, relay, unrolled-relay and lookahead adders at 8 and 16 bits.
- All 21 return to the loaded net agent for agent.
- So do 8,000 random terms, which also agree with an independent tree-calculus evaluator.
parallelism_locality:
**Local.** Every step is two agents joined by one wire, plus free slots in one 2×2×2 block. The wire is one of:
- front to front, for a meeting;
- E's front on an output, for collecting;
- back port to child port, for absorbing;
- trail to front, for an exchange.

Nothing reads a table, an id or a far position.

**Parallel:**
- Each agent has one front port, so ready meetings are disjoint and all fire at once.
- Backward steps at different footprints are disjoint. One footprint takes its products back one at a time, or all at once if they are in its block.
- The only conflict is an agent that could go either forward or back; the drive decides.
- Since every law except commit is injective and every backward move leads to a state that some forward order also reaches, backward moves never wander off the forward path (Melgratti et al.'s condition).

**How it was measured.** Prototype in /tmp/fpnet, abstract rounds, one simple scheduler used for both tables:
- demand flows from the root through front ports and every apply's argument, so both halves of each S rule are wanted;
- collectors are always active;
- what a round makes waits for the next round.

Absolute rounds are therefore not rev.rs's (the event-log engine): the same current table takes 873 rounds here for add 2 3, against rev.rs's 631. Only the ratios are comparable.

**Results:**

| quantity | ratio | geometric mean |
|---|---|---|
| forward rounds vs the current 26-rule table | 0.94–1.08× | 1.02× |
| forward meetings vs the current table | 0.94–1.04× | 1.02× |
| backward rounds, one product per footprint per round (the lattice regime) | 0.55–1.09× forward | 0.81× |
| backward rounds, whole undos per round (rev.rs's regime) | 0.28–0.55× forward | 0.40× |

- Widest forward round: 12 → 15 (add 2 3), 36 → 36 (fib 3), 52 → 92 (relay 65535+1).
- Widest backward round: 171–3,058.

**Against earlier designs:**
- **The walkers (tck walker)** took 9.4–51× the net's rounds (add 1 1: 3,939 against 418; 16-bit relay: 32,835 against 685), with 4–9 tokens. This core keeps the net's width going forward and is at least as parallel going back.
- **The substrate** (the lattice run as physics) goes back in 10–12× its forward clocks, because an undo needs every product in one block at once. Here every undo is a two-agent meeting along a wire, the same physics as a forward meeting. Predicted: back ≈ 1–2× forward clocks. This is not measured on the lattice.
- **Exchange code** (the binary adder) is one walker: 2n+1 sequential steps.

**Space.** Live agents peak at 1.00–1.21× the current table. With every footprint kept, matter peaks at 6.2–8.1× (1.7× for the unrolled relay).
lattice_physical:
**Strand lattice:**
- Agents sit in slots as now. Each gains a back port.
- A footprint is an agent seated in one of the two slots its pair frees. It has at most 6 wire ends with everything out, and up to 10 while partly taken back.
- Back wires are strand paths like any wire.

**Moves,** each inside one 2×2×2 block:
- meet + emit: today's rewrite, with the footprint seated where the pair was, products in free slots, and back strands of length at most 1;
- absorb: a product one strand from its footprint along its back wire;
- part;
- exchange;
- commit;
- step, exchange, fold and flip, unchanged.

**Energy:**
- A meet costs −ε (the drive); a part costs +ε.
- Driven forward, tension is on front wires. Driven backward, it is on back wires. This replaces the substrate's bonds: the pull runs along a real path, with no position read and no gathering toward a centroid.
- Fuel is free slots, so copying waits for room, as now.
- Heat is a particle per committed footprint that diffuses to the edge. This makes fuel and heat local fields, the README's open item.

**Reversible block substrate.** Meet, emit, absorb, part and exchange are each bijections on block states, because a footprint's kind names its rule and which products are out. So:
- With Margolus's alternating blocks, the whole lattice is invertible when the block map is.
- One clock bit per site (shown by Margolus in 1D, plausible for 2×2×2) gives asynchronous updates with synchronous causality.
- Creutz demons (a small energy counter per site) replace Metropolis acceptance, which is not a bijection.

Conserved in every block:
- slots: agents plus vacuum;
- back wiring: every back port is wired to exactly one footprint, or capped;
- energy: demons plus ε.

No state merges except at commit, so a tiny drive suffices, as for Bennett's unbranched computation. Only the meeting is biased, matching Brownian circuits, where the join is the only element producing environment entropy.

**Quantum.** Block permutations are permutation unitaries. Commit is the one step that needs an environment: heat particles leaving through the edge. Copying is defined only in the classical basis.

weaknesses: History is as big as the run: one footprint per rewrite, 8.7–37× the loaded program (1.7× for the unrolled relay). If all of it is kept, peak matter is 6.2–8.1× the current table's. It shrinks only by going back (time) or by committing (heat). Running back the branches that missed the answer removes only 20–31%: when a collector reaches a duplicator's unused output and turns it into a relay, the value that relay passes on depends on the collector, so collection becomes part of the answer's causal past.

Heat: committing blindly and locally costs about one unit per rewrite, no better per step than an irreversible machine. The Landauer floor is far lower: the 24–83 dropped originals per run, and about 0 for a history whose input is kept. Reaching it needs erasure that sees both sides at once (running back, or checking twins side by side), and that is sequential.

Bennett's clean-up (copy the answer, then run back) cannot be done inside the net, because reading uses agents up. Results that leave no history need exchange code, which is one walker per list and so sequential. This angle makes the trade plain: running many things at once creates history.

name: Loan net: room is borrowed, heat is spent
angle: Resources first. Clean space is fuel that a run borrows and has to give back. Forgetting is heat that it spends at the lattice's edge. History is a borrowed workspace (catalytic computing, dirty ancillae, compute-copy-uncompute, pebbling as a schedule). So the core keeps no log at all. A copy that has not been made yet is a loan, and dropping it repays the loan. A pending operation is its own undo record. A reversible add borrows everything it uses and returns it.
summary:
My angle comes down to something small, and it is mostly deletions. Keep the lazy tree-calculus net that the strand lattice already runs. Use rules.rs's 26 rules minus the six for suspensions, which demand makes redundant. Change only two things: what is counted and what is kept.

1. Room is borrowed. An empty seat is fuel. A step that makes more agents than it uses takes seats in its 2×2×2 block, and waits if there are none (the lattice already does this). A step that makes fewer agents gives seats back. When the run ends, every seat is back except the ones the answer occupies.
2. Heat is spent. No step is recorded. Each step forgets its own record immediately and pays one drive quantum into a 4-bit energy counter on its site (a Creutz demon, i.e. a local energy bank). Counters pass quanta to their neighbours, and the lattice's edge drains them to a bath. The edge is the only irreversible place. Erasing a tree costs one step per node.
3. A duplicator that has not copied yet is a loan. When an eraser reaches it, the eraser repays it in one step and the copy is never built. This is the lattice's existing collection with a price attached. A copied layer that is dropped later gets erased node by node, because no local process can tell it apart from unique data.
4. There is one new 3-port agent, append. It walks a list's spine and puts a tail where the last leaf was.
   - A loan of a that feeds an append gives (a, b) → (a, a+b) on disp's unary numbers in 3a+2 steps, with nothing left over.
   - Append alone is disp's add with a not kept: a+1 steps and no copying.
   - While the sum has not been read, un-append hands b back and repays the loan in two steps.

History is whatever is still pending: loans, applications that are waiting, and appends that have not walked yet. Reading a result spends it.

What gets deleted:
- the substrate's machinery (phys=1, the lattice run as physics): records, ids, marks, bonds, gathering, cascading forgets, magic record kinds and the global ledger;
- the global temperature and the cooling phase;
- the copy-ahead threshold (dnroom).

What is given up: rewinding ordinary programs exactly.
primitives:
Matter (the "fermions"):
- L, a leaf [p]
- S, a stem [p, child]
- F, a fork [p, left, right]

disp's numbers are n forks over a leaf (0 = L, n+1 = F(L, n)). Bits are b0 = L and b1 = S(L).

Mediators (the "bosons"), taken unchanged from rust-ca-lattice/crate/src/rules.rs:
- A, apply [p = function, z, res]
- T, first-level triage (rules.rs T1) [p = a, arms, res]
- D, second-level dispatch (rules.rs Sel) [p = z, arms, res]
- Pr, the pair that carries the arms [p, 1, 2]
- U, unpair [p, 1, 2]
- Dn, the loan, i.e. the lazy duplicator [p = source, c1, c2]
- E, the eraser [p]
- N, the normalizer [p, res], and the root; together they read the answer out.

New:
- Ap, append [p = the list, res, tail]
- Un, un-append [p, res]

Fields:
- Each seat holds one agent or is empty. An empty seat is room, which is the fuel.
- Each site holds a demon d in 0..15. That is its heat quanta (Creutz's energy bank).
- Sites, strands, switchboards, demand pulses and fork stay exactly as the strand lattice has them.

Removed:
- P, the suspension. The loader writes each application as an A that waits for demand, which is what the run already does for the applications it makes. The README notes that duplicators never meet a suspension during a run.
- Seam.
- Everything the substrate attached to agents: ids, record numbers, marks and bonds.

Superpositions and movement agents are independent of this design. They are allowed but not needed.
rules:
Notation: ports are listed principal first. Each rule reads "meeting → what is made [room = agents made − agents used]", followed by pinned or closing. Every rule is a rules.rs-style template whose wires form a perfect matching, which validate() checks. A rule runs forward by paying a drive quantum into its site's demon, and backward by taking one out.
- Pinned: the reverse can start only from what this step made, so a small drive is enough.
- Closing: the reverse could start wherever the right side's shape appears in the block (any stem, any two wires, and so on). The drive then has to be about kT ln of that count (Bennett).

Apply and dispatch (rules.rs RULES minus its six P rules):
1. A·L → S(z) at res [−1] closing.
2. A·S(a) → F(a, z) at res [−1] closing.
3. A·F(a, b) → T on a, with arms Pr⟨b, z⟩ [0] pinned.
4. K: T·L → U on the arms; U.1 (b) → res; U.2 (z) → E [0] pinned.
5. S rule: T·S(s) → U on the arms (b, z); z → Dn; A(s, Dn.c2), A(b, Dn.c1), and A(first, second) → res [+3] pinned.
6. T·F(w, x) → U on the arms (b, z); z → D with arms Pr⟨w, Pr⟨x, b⟩⟩ [+2] pinned.
7. D·L → U on the arms: w → res, ⟨x, b⟩ → E [0] pinned.
8. D·S(u) → U, U: w → E, b → E, A(x, u) → res [+3] pinned.
9. D·F(u, v) → U, U: w → E, x → E, A(A(b, u), v) → res [+4] pinned.
10. U·Pr → both wire pairs joined [−2] closing.

Loans:
11. Dn·L → L at c1, L at c2 [0] closing. The loan is paid off at a leaf.
12. Dn·S(u) → S at c1, S at c2, with a Dn on u under both [+1] pinned.
13. Dn·F(l, r) → F at c1, F at c2, Dn on l, Dn on r [+2] pinned.

Erasing. The node's kind also goes into the demon as 1, 2 or 3 quanta for L, S or F. This is where structure becomes heat.
14. E·L → nothing [−2] closing.
15. E·S(u) → E on u [−1] closing.
16. E·F(l, r) → E on l, E on r [0] closing.
17. E·Pr → E on each half [0] closing. A pair is scaffolding, so it has no kind.

Reading the answer:
18. N·L → L at res [−1] closing.
19. N·S(u) → S at res, N on u [0] pinned.
20. N·F(l, r) → F at res, N on l, N on r [+1] pinned.

Contacts. An eraser or un-append touches a non-principal port of a waiting agent, the same way the lattice's collection works today.
21. Repay: E at Dn.c_i → Dn's source joined to Dn.c_(3−i) [−2] closing. The copy is never built.
22. Dead work: E at the res of an A, T, D or Ap → an E on each of its other two partners [0] closing.
23. Unpaired: E on both outputs of a U → one E on its input [−2] closing.

Append (new):
24. Ap·L → res joined to tail [−2] closing.
25. Ap·S(u) → S at res, whose child comes from the next Ap's res; that Ap sits on u with the same tail [0] pinned.
26. Ap·F(l, v) → F at res with left child l and right child from the next Ap's res; that Ap sits on v with the same tail [0] pinned.
27. Un-append: Un at the res of an Ap that is still waiting on its list → Un.res joined to the Ap's tail; E on the Ap's input [−1] closing.

Moves: the strand lattice's step, exchange, fold and flip are accepted against the block's demon instead of against a temperature. There is one new move: a heat quantum passes to a neighbouring site's demon.

Rules whose right sides have the same shape (4 and 7; 21 and 24) put different amounts into the demon. That keeps the block map one-to-one until the heat mixes.

The one irreversible step is the edge drain. Edge sites' demons exchange quanta with an outside bath held at the bath temperature. While the lattice is hotter than the bath, net heat flows out. Every quantum a run spends is finally paid there.
resources:
Room is borrowed, heat is spent.

Room (fuel):
- Room is the empty seats of a block. Each rule's room change is fixed by its template (see the rule list):
  - the S rule takes +3, a copied fork +2, a copied stem +1, and triage scaffolding +2 to +4;
  - builds give back 1, fusions 2, erasing a leaf 2 and erasing a stem 1, a repay 2, and an append's last step 2.
- A step that needs room waits for it.
- By the end of a run every seat is back except the answer's. So room is a loan the run repays, and its peak is the run's space. This is Fredkin and Toffoli's scratchpad, which provides "spare room rather than tokens".

Heat (spent):
- Each step puts one drive quantum into its site's demon. It comes back only if a fluctuation undoes that step.
- Demons pass quanta to their neighbours, and the edge drains them.
- A pinned step can run on a fraction of a quantum. A closing step needs about kT ln of how many places its reverse could start.

Deleting is paid in steps:
- Erasing a tree of n nodes takes n steps, and each puts the node's kind into the demon.
- A dropped copy that was never built costs one repay step for the whole copy.
- So forgetting costs in proportion to what a local process can see. A waiting duplicator "knows" its two outputs are equal, because they are still one wire. A finished copy that has drifted away from its twin does not.

Copying draws room and buys parallelism:
- Only the S rule's loan copies. A loan copies a layer when a reader takes it. It copies ahead of the reader only where its block has spare room and a cool demon. This is dnroom (copying ahead where a block has room) made physical: today it gives 0.82× the clocks for 1.68× the rewrites, and about 2–5× the erasing later.
- Where room runs short, copying waits, and more loans are repaid before anything is built.
- Ackley's "reproduce only by transmuting Res atoms" is the same brake on runaway copying.

Reusing instead of copying:
- A loan shares a value until each reader actually takes a layer.
- Over the 27 programs, code is copied 109,171 times for 75,990 uses, and only 6–33% of the copies are needed at the same time. Repaying and waiting are where the savings are.
- 83–96% of S firings are B/C shapes whose copy K drops right away. Each of those becomes one repay step.
- Append moves data instead of copying it.
- Movement agents, if added, route arguments with no loan at all and halve the steps, which halves the heat.

The bill, run lazily on the lattice: add 2 3 costs about 2,100 steps of heat and 160 erase rewrites (786 when copying ahead). By REVERSIBLE_PIPELINE.md's measurements, only about 25 agents' worth of information is really lost. The drive is most of the bill. Forgetting is the part that shows what the program threw away.
history_as_resource:
The core keeps no log. Nothing about what has already happened is recorded anywhere. Its history is what has not happened yet, and that is matter a run borrows and returns:
- A loan (a duplicator that has not copied) is a copy promised to two readers. If one of them drops its copy first, an eraser repays the loan in one step and the copy is never built. This is Bennett's reversible un-copy of "one of two copies of data known to be identical". Here "known" is literal: the duplicator still joins the two copies.
- A waiting application is a frame of the continuation (the rest of the computation). It is used up when its argument or result arrives.
- A pending append is the record of an addition. While the sum is unread, un-append undoes it in two steps.

A pending operation is its own undo record, and reading its result spends that record. After that, the only way back is to compute again. That is Bennett's point that a cleanup machine can only erase the garbage of the machine it inverts.

Programs use this in three ways:
1. A reversible add leaves nothing. The loan and the append are both used up as a and a+b are read.
2. Try-and-undo is free. Add, then un-append before anything reads the sum: this costs nothing, and every seat comes back.
3. Laziness is the pebbling schedule. A value is copied when a second reader takes it, copied ahead of time only where a block has spare room and is cool, and never copied if a reader drops it first. Removing a pebble is either a repay (no copy was ever made) or an erasure (heat). Recomputing is not used.

In Bennett's terms, compute-copy-uncompute becomes lend-read-repay. In catalytic computing's terms, the borrowed workspace is room, and it has to come back exactly; the core counts it. The only dirty workspace a program may borrow is its own data, the way Cuccaro's adder parks carries in a's bits (see binary add).

What a run did is not kept. Each step forgets its record immediately and pays heat for that. It is the same unit the substrate charges when it forgets a record later (2,300–6,600 records per call), only paid at once instead of carried around. The substrate kept what had been done so it could go back. The loan net keeps only what is still to be done, which is why it needs no table.
reversible_add:
Unary, using disp's numbers (0 = L, n+1 = F(L, n)).

(a, b) → (a, a+b) takes two agents: a loan Dn[source a; c1 → a-out, c2 → x] and an append Ap[list x; res → sum-out, tail b]. The primitive's apply rule (or the loader) spawns them.

Example: a = 2 = F(L, F(L, L)), b = 1 = F(L, L). Rule numbers refer to the rule list.
0. Spawn Dn and Ap [room +2]. The sum is wanted, so Ap is wanted, and its demand reaches the loan.
1. Dn·F (13): an F at a-out, an F at x, a loan on a's left leaf and a loan on a' = F(L, L) [+2].
2. Ap·F (26) on x's F: it is re-emitted at the sum, and the next Ap goes on its right child [0]. In the same round the left loan pays off with Dn·L (11) [0].
3. Dn·F (13) on a' [+2].
4. Ap·F (26) and Dn·L (11) again [0].
5. Dn·L (11) at a's last leaf: one L ends a-out and one ends x [0].
6. Ap·L (24): b joins where x's last leaf was [−2].

End state:
- a-out = F(L, F(L, L)) = 2 and sum = F(L, F(L, F(L, L))) = 3.
- Left over: nothing. No other agent remains, no eraser ever ran, and nothing was recorded.
- Room borrowed: 4 = 2a, exactly the forks and leaves the sum has beyond b.
- Heat: 3a + 2 = 8 steps. The 2a loan and append steps are pinned (their reverse can only start where they ended), so they could creep forward on almost no drive. Only the a + 1 leaf payoffs and the final join are closing steps.
- Time: about 2a + 2 rounds lazily, or a + 2 if the loan copies ahead.

The inverse reuses the add's own history. Before the sum is read (the Ap is still waiting on the loan), Un at the sum (27) hands b back and puts an eraser on x. The eraser repays the loan (21). That returns exactly (a, b), with every seat back, in two steps. Once the sum has been read, the junction is spent, and subtracting is ordinary code that pays per node.

disp's own add, where a is not kept, is the append alone: Ap[a; res, b]. It takes a + 1 steps, room −1 (a's last leaf comes back), and copies nothing. For comparison, add 2 3:
- compiled to tree calculus on the net: 2,658 rewrites in 631 rounds;
- tck (the tree calculus that keeps the applied program): 8,693 moves in 6,197 rounds;
- the two-way calculus's library add: 29 moves by one token.

Why only these two shapes? A step that keeps a and changes b has two inputs and two outputs. A net whose agents have three ports can only do that as a loan of a (one in, two out) followed by a merge into b (two in, one out). That is exactly Dn then Ap. Theseus's add (one register counts up while the other counts down) and Janus's b += a (with b not in the expression) have the same shape.

Binary (bits least significant first, b0 = L, b1 = S(L), a number is a list of bits). This core has no history-free binary add.
- The carries are binary add's history. The core offers the three prices the pebbling literature names: keep them (one bit of matter each), forget them (one eraser per dropped carry, paid in heat), or uncompute them.
- Uncomputing them is Cuccaro's adder:
  - Going toward the high end, MAJ (c, b, a) → (c⊕a, b⊕a, maj(a, b, c)) parks each carry in a's own cell.
  - Coming back, UMA restores a and c and writes the sum bit into b's cell.
  - Nothing is left: the single carry ancilla returns to b0, in 2n column steps. a's bits are the dirty workspace it borrows and returns.
- Cuccaro's column does not factor as a loan followed by a merge, because each column is three bits in and three out, in place. As agents it would need:
  - a walker with two carry states;
  - spine nodes that the walker turns around as it passes, so it can climb back without a stack;
  - reading two cells per column.
  That is about six agent kinds and sixteen rules. I left it out rather than pretend it is small.
- Today relay_add (programs.disp's binary adder) runs as ordinary code and pays per node it forgets. relay_add 13 6 erases about 700 nodes lazily, against about 95 agents' worth of information really lost.
tree_calculus:
disp's compiled trees run unchanged on rules 1–20, with fork (both halves of the S rule run) and demand working as they do now. The loader builds the program and its arguments as matter, and builds each application as an apply that waits for demand.

- Apply (1–3): A·L and A·S build a stem and a fork. These lose nothing but are closing steps. A·F opens the function into a T on its left child with the arms Pr⟨b, z⟩ (pinned, room 0).
- K (4): T·L keeps b and hands z to an eraser, which walks into z.
  - At a waiting duplicator it repays the loan (21): one step, and the copy is never built.
  - At an application's result it stops that work (22).
  - At a node it erases it (14–16): one step per node, with the node's kind going into the demon.
  - Since 83–96% of S firings are B/C shapes whose copy K drops right away, most K drops cost one repay.
- S (5): T·S(s) gives s z (b z), with z lent through a loan.
  - This is the only place a program borrows room for copying, one layer at a time as the two readers take it, or ahead of them where a block has room and is cool.
  - It is also the only source of new parallel work: code that copies itself makes more places where rewrites can happen.
- Triage (6–9): T·F(w, x) dispatches on z through a D with arms ⟨w, ⟨x, b⟩⟩. D·L, D·S and D·F keep one arm and hand the other two to erasers. Those are mostly copies of code, so they are repaid.
  - Which arm was taken is recorded nowhere. That information goes into the D step's drive, since its reverse could have started from any of the three shapes.
  - Abramsky shows that a built-in conditional is exactly where history-free reversibility fails.
- Fusions (10) and a loan's payoff at a leaf (11) are closing steps and pay the drive.

What a run leaves: the answer and nothing else.

What a run spends: one drive quantum per step. For add 2 3 that is about 2,100 steps lazily and about 3,400 when copying ahead.
- Of these, the erase rewrites are the price of forgetting:

  | call | erase rewrites, lazy | erase rewrites, copying ahead | information really lost |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | add 2 3 | 160 | 786 | about 25 agents' worth |
  | relay_add 13 6 | 876 | 1,825 | about 95 |
  | fib 3 | 1,675 | 3,440 | — |
  | fib 2 | — | — | about 112 |

- The gap between erasing and information lost is copies that were erased far from their twins.
- 75–84% of rewrites lose nothing, so the drive, not forgetting, is most of the bill.

Movement agents fit in unchanged in resource terms. B, C and I steps are pure moves, a K view drops (it hands off to an eraser), and Sx and W lend. They halve the steps (0.55×), and so they halve the heat.
parallelism_locality:
Local:
- Every rule fires inside one 2×2×2 block. Either two agents' principal ports meet, or (rules 21–23 and 27) an eraser or un-append touches a waiting agent's port in the same site or the next, as collection does today.
- The demon is per site. Heat moves one quantum at a time to a neighbour. The drain touches only edge sites.
- There are no ids, no table, no distance reads, and no cascades. (The substrate's bond energy read seat_of across the whole lattice.)
- Bilardi and Preparata's condition for a machine that scales strictly holds: its cells are nameless and finite-state.

Parallel:
- The computing rules are the lazy net's, so the width is the net's. In strict rounds:

  | call | rounds | widest round |
  |---|---|---|
  | add 2 3 | 631 | 12 |
  | fib 3 | 1,324 | 36 |
  | relay_add 8-bit | 517 | 74 |
  | relay_add 16-bit | 685 | 144 |

  That is 4.2–23.7 rewrites per round. The walker machines managed 1.4–1.8 moves per round and took 9.4–51× as many rounds.
- Nothing is added to the critical path. There are no records to write or undo. (The substrate costs 8–17% more clocks going forward, from undo-and-redo churn, and 10–12× the clocks to go back.) Demons change only on moves that happen anyway.
- Copying and erasing add width, not depth: counting them as free shortens the causal chain by only 5–11%. So pricing them changes the bill, not the time.

The reversible primitives are chains, not walkers:
- A loan plus an append adds in about 2a + 2 rounds and 3a + 2 steps.
- The loan's new layer arrives in the block where the append is waiting. Readers already meet their copies 1–4 strands away.
- Many appends run at once on independent data. A unary add is sequential only because the number itself is a chain.
- The only exact inverses (repay and un-append) involve two agents already joined by a wire, which is the cheap case: points joined by a chain meet in about the chain's relaxation time (Guérin et al.). The substrate's undos needed up to six agents together in one block, and that is where its 10–12× came from.

Limits: heat leaves only through the surface. Sustained width × drive must stay below what the edge can drain, which is O(L²) per clock for an L³ lattice (Frank's surface limit). A wide run, such as relay_add 16-bit at about 150 rewrites per round, heats its middle and slows itself down. The first experiment measures how soon that happens.
lattice_physical:
On the strand lattice:
- Kept: sites, strands, switchboards, the four moves, demand pulses and fork.
- Added: a 4-bit demon per site (about 4% on top of the roughly 95 bits a site holds now), a heat move (one quantum to a neighbour inside the block) and the edge drain.
- Changed:
  - Metropolis acceptance at a global temperature becomes Creutz acceptance against the block's demon. A move that raises the energy by Δ takes Δ from the demon; a move that lowers it gives Δ back.
  - The end-of-run cooling phase becomes heat draining out once rewrites stop.
  - The copy-ahead threshold becomes "copy ahead where the block has room and its demon is below a set level".
- Tags: Ap and Un come in, P and Seam go out, so the tags still fit the chip's 4 bits, and 27 rules fit its 5-bit rule field.
- Each rule is a template validated as a perfect matching, so the GPU's and the chip's block updates stay local to 8 sites.

On a reversible block substrate:
- Each clock is a product of block maps. The dice are already a hash of site and clock, so running the same table with the clock decreasing gives the inverse schedule.
- Creutz acceptance is a bijection on (configuration, demon).
- A rewrite is a bijection between its two sides, with its drive moved into or out of the demon.
- An eraser's step turns a node into demon quanta, and the amount tells the node's kind. Rules whose right sides look alike deposit different amounts.
- So every step inside the lattice is a permutation of block states, which is Margolus's condition (the block rule is one-to-one).
- The information a run forgets sits in demon quanta until it mixes and leaves through the open edge. This is how D'Souza and Margolus's growth model stores "when and where" in its heat particles. The edge is the one element that is not a bijection, and Landauer's price is paid there.

On a quantum substrate:
- The same block permutations are permutation unitaries on alternating cuts (Schumacher and Werner). The demons are qudits, and the edge is the environment.
- Copying exists only in the computational basis, so a duplicator under a superposed value entangles rather than copies (no-cloning).
- Pati and Braunstein's no-deleting result says un-copying an unknown state is only a swap into the ancilla, so repay is a classical-basis operation.

weaknesses: It gives up rewinding ordinary programs. The substrate brings any run back to the loaded net agent for agent; here only what is still pending can be undone (repay, un-append), and the player's time bar still needs saved states.

Copies erased far from their twins cost heat like unique data. add 2 3 erases 161 nodes lazily, 145 of them copies, against about 25 agents' worth of information really lost, and copying ahead multiplies erasing about 2-5x. A local process cannot do better (a copy erased by a separate gate adds its full entropy to the loss); only laziness narrows the gap.

The drive, not forgetting, dominates the heat: about 2,100 steps against 160 erase rewrites for add 2 3. With no records, a closing step's reverse can start anywhere in its block, so each one needs a few kT. Cutting heat means cutting steps (movement agents, primitives), not erasing more cleverly.

The two-way layer is tiny. Loans and append give unary add and subtract, list append and copying, but not binary add (Cuccaro's column step would add about six agent kinds and sixteen rules) and not general bijections. A core that forgets nothing reaches exactly the injective functions; this one, without its forgetting, reaches much less.

disp code reaches append only through the loader: a definition marked in .opt.disp (add, append) is swapped for append-based agents, the way movement agents replace B/C shapes. A program that triages such a primitive needs its whole tree spelled out (hundreds of nodes), which a single 2x2x2 rule cannot do.
Un-append works only while the sum is unread. After that, subtraction is ordinary code and pays per node.

Creutz demons change the movement dynamics the lattice was tuned on: tension, crowding and idle repulsion would be paid from local demons instead of a global temperature. This is untested. Hot spots near wide forks may slow walkers and let data un-build briefly; those fluctuations are harmless and fire again, but they waste moves.
Heat leaves only through the surface, so a wide run throttles itself in its middle. The core makes this visible; it does not avoid it.
Dropping suspensions assumes demand reaches every application the loader writes, as it already does for the ones the run makes. The abstract net used for checking has no demand and would need it too.

The tree rules are not clash-free: K and the leaf dispatch leave the same shape, and fusions and erasures leave shapes that occur anyway. So strict one-to-one block maps rely on those rules putting different amounts into the demon. The pinned/closing split of the drive is Bennett's branching rule applied rule by rule and is not yet measured; a first version would use one drive for every step.
